attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: 'Even now, no software would be able to' is a firm claim about present capability, not a hedge or a forecast. The proposition dated December 2023 is faithful.

contract.note: The plain reading (reliable comprehension across varied videos, not perfection) is fair and ordinary. Because the challenge has no dataset or threshold, the result depends on that interpretation.

evidence.note: MovieChat preprint dated Dec 3, 2023. It reports progress on long videos and admits limits, but it is not a full test of the challenge and covers one system.
Google's Dec 6, 2023 blog shows prompted image-sequence demos that sometimes fail. These are selected examples, not an evaluation of the challenge.

reviews.rationale: Neither item measures the full Comprehension Challenge for all contemporary software. MovieChat's admitted limits and Gemini's demo failures fit Marcus's claim but do not establish that no system could pass. Nothing shows any system passing either. The packet does not settle the universal claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: A firm observation that nobody was close to passing the Comprehension Challenge. Reading the Gemini aside as dismissing the demos, not exempting Gemini, is reasonable.

contract.note: 'Close' has no threshold. The contract's reading (reliable performance over most of the challenge, with only limited gaps) is ordinary and fair, but the result depends on it.

evidence.note: MovieChat preprint dated Dec 3, 2023, with long-video progress and stated limits. It does not measure how close it is to a human-level standard.
MVBench preprint dated Nov 28, 2023. A sampled multiple-choice GPT-4V comparison, too narrow to measure closeness to passing the open-ended challenge.
Gemini 1.0 report dated Dec 19, 2023, about systems that existed by Dec 9. Strong benchmark results on 16 sampled frames, but no human-viewer standard for the full challenge.

reviews.rationale: The evidence shows narrow benchmark progress plus admitted limits, with no human baseline across the challenge's breadth. It neither shows every leading system was far from passing nor shows any system was close. The packet does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words, citing the Jones and Bergen paper.

semantics.note: Correctly limited to the cited study. 'Beat' is read through the study's overall success rate.

contract.note: Using the overall judged-human rate in the cited v1 paper is the natural reading of 'beat' given his citation.

evidence.note: v1 of the paper (Oct 31, 2023) reports ELIZA at a 27% success rate and GPT-3.5 at 5% to 14%. The authors say ELIZA outperformed all GPT-3.5 witnesses.

reviews.rationale: The cited study's overall success rates put ELIZA (27%) above every GPT-3.5 configuration (5% to 14%). This meets the support condition. ELIZA's lower first-game rate is a side analysis, not the overall measure.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Rightly limited to the AI witnesses in the cited study, without the added 'test not solved' conclusion.

contract.note: Comparing the human witnesses with every AI configuration on the study's success rate is a fair reading of 'ahead' given the citation.

evidence.note: v1 of the paper reports human witnesses at a 63% success rate. The best AI, GPT-4 Sierra, reached 41%, and all others scored lower.

reviews.rationale: In the cited study, human witnesses (63%) had a higher success rate than every tested AI configuration (41% at best). This meets the support condition.
